prompt: In https://login.examplebank.com.account-check.net/sign-in, which part shows who owns the site?
options: login.examplebank.com
account-check.net
/sign-in
https://
explanation: Read from the right and stop at the first single slash. The site belongs to account-check.net, and everything in front of it is decoration.

prompt: A colleague says a page must be genuine because it shows a padlock. What is the best reply?
options: That is correct, the padlock proves it
The padlock only means the connection is encrypted, and fake sites can have one too
That is correct if the padlock is green
That is correct if the page looks professional
explanation: The padlock protects data in transit. It does not tell you who runs the site.

prompt: Your password manager offers no login on a page that looks exactly like your email provider's. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The password manager is broken
The address is not the one you saved, so the page may be fake
The page is loading slowly
The password manager only works at night
explanation: A password manager only fills logins on the exact saved address. Its silence is a useful warning.

prompt: An email says: 'Your session has expired. Sign in again.' It includes a link. What is the best action?
options: Click it and sign in
Open the site yourself, using a bookmark or by typing the address
Reply and ask if it is real
Click it but use a different browser
explanation: A different browser does not help. Reach the site yourself, so you never depend on a link an attacker chose.

prompt: Which address is most likely a lookalike of examplebank.com?
options: examp1ebank.com
www.examplebank.com
examplebank.com
help.examplebank.com
explanation: The number 1 replaces the letter l. The www and help versions still end in examplebank.com, so they belong to the same owner.

prompt: You click a link in a message and your browser shows a full-page 'Deceptive site ahead' warning. What should you do?
options: Click through, because browsers are overcautious
Close the page and report the message
Turn off the warning in settings
Refresh until the warning goes away
explanation: These warnings are triggered by known malicious pages. Close the page, and report the message that led you there.

prompt: A QR code sticker has been placed over the original on a parking meter, and it says 'Scan to pay'. What is the safest option?
options: Scan it quickly and pay
Use the operator's official app or website, and report the sticker
Scan it, but do not type card details
Scan it with a second phone
explanation: A QR code hides its address, and a pasted sticker is a warning sign. Use an official app or website you trust.

prompt: Why are shortened links risky when they arrive unexpectedly?
options: They hide the real destination
They always contain malware
They are slower to load
They cannot be opened on phones
explanation: You cannot judge a destination you cannot see. Treat an unexpected short link as an unknown address.
